 }}</ref> named after its authors [[Danny Dolev]] and [[Andrew Yao]], is a [[Mathematical model|formal model]] used to prove properties of interactive  cryptographic protocols.<ref>{{Citation

==The network==

The network is represented by a set of abstract machines that can exchange messages.
These messages consist of formal terms. These terms reveal some of the internal structure of the messages, but some parts will hopefully remain opaque to the adversary.

==The adversary==

The adversary in this model can overhear, intercept, and synthesize any message and is only limited by the constraints of the cryptographic methods used. In other words: "the attacker carries the message."

This [[omnipotence]] has been very difficult to model, and many threat models simplify it, as has been done for the attacker in [[ubiquitous computing]].<ref name="Creese">{{cite tech report
  | last1 = Creese | first1 = Sadie
  | last2 = Goldsmith | first2 = Michael
  | last3 = Roscoe | first3 = Bill
  | last4 = Zakiuddin | first4 = Irfan
  | title = The Attacker in Ubiquitous Computing Environments: Formalising the Threat Model
  | work = Proc. of the 1st Intl Workshop on Formal Aspects in Security and Trust
  | year = 2003
  | pages = 83-97
  | url = https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/37832178.pdf#page=87
}}</ref>

==The algebraic model==

[[Cryptographic primitive]]s are modeled by abstract operators. For example, asymmetric encryption for a user <math>x</math> is represented by the encryption function <math>E_x</math> and the decryption function <math>D_x</math>. Their main properties are that their composition is the [[identity function]] (<math>D_x E_x = E_x D_x = 1</math>) and that an encrypted message <math>E_x(M)</math> reveals nothing about <math>M</math>. Unlike in the real world, the adversary can neither manipulate the encryption's bit representation nor guess the key. The attacker may, however, re-use any messages that have been sent and therefore become known. The attacker can encrypt or decrypt these with any keys he knows, to forge subsequent messages.

A protocol is modeled as a set of sequential runs, alternating between queries (sending a message over the network) and responses (obtaining a message from the network).

===Remark===

The symbolic nature of the Dolev–Yao model makes it more manageable than computational models and accessible to [[algebra]]ic methods but potentially less realistic. However, both kinds of models for cryptographic protocols have been related.<ref name="Herzog">{{Citation
  | title = A Computational Interpretation of Dolev-Yao Adversaries
  | last1 = Herzog | first1 = Jonathan
  | journal = Theoretical Computer Science
  | volume = 340 | issue = 1 | pages = 57–81
  | year = 2005
  | doi = 10.1016/j.tcs.2005.03.003
 }}</ref> Also, symbolic models are very well suited to show that a protocol is ''broken'', rather than secure, under the given assumptions about the attacker's capabilities.
